title: Floating-point addition
intro: Catch up on the key A Level ideas. Complete four retrieval questions, work through the examples, then practise and explain your reasoning.

questions.prompt: Encode 0.375 in normalised 8-bit mantissa, 4-bit exponent format.
Convert eight-bit two’s complement 11110110 to denary.
Convert AD hexadecimal to binary, then logically shift right once. What is the final denary value?

blocks.title: Format and method
blocks.text: Use a six-bit two’s-complement mantissa and four-bit two’s-complement exponent unless stated otherwise. Mantissa weights are −1, ½, ¼, ⅛, 1/16, 1/32. Align exponents → add signed mantissas with extra working width → normalise → check precision and range.

blocks.title: Worked example: align 5 + 1.5
blocks.text: 5 = 010100 0011; 1.5 = 011000 0001. Use exponent 3. Increase the second exponent from 1 to 3 and arithmetic-right-shift its mantissa twice: 011000 → 001100 → 000110. It still represents 1.5 at exponent 3.

blocks.title: Worked example: add and normalise
blocks.text: Sign-extend both aligned mantissas to seven working bits: 0010100 + 0000110 = 0011010. Remove the redundant extra working sign bit to return to six bits: 011010. This is already normalised. Result: 011010 0011 = 6.5.

blocks.title: Negative values and rescaling
blocks.text: Arithmetic right shifts repeat the sign bit: a negative mantissa receives 1 on the left. For 6 + 5 at exponent 3, widened mantissas give 0011000 + 0010100 = 0101100. The sum is too large for a six-bit mantissa: rescale right once and increase exponent to 4. Store 010110 0100 = 11.

blocks.title: Keep precision until the final result
blocks.text: Guard bits retain low-order working digits during alignment. They reduce premature precision loss but cannot make an unrepresentable final result exact. At exponent 6, adjacent six-bit positive mantissas differ in value by 2. Therefore 32.5 cannot be stored exactly. Use the rounding or truncation rule specified.

questions.prompt: Why align exponents before adding mantissas?
questions.answer: So corresponding bits have the same scaled place values
questions.feedback: Without alignment, the bit columns represent different amounts.
options: So corresponding bits have the same scaled place values

questions.prompt: Which bit enters on the left when a negative mantissa is arithmetic-right-shifted?
questions.feedback: Repeat the sign bit to preserve a negative sign.

questions.prompt: How many working bits are used when adding a temporary extra sign bit to a six-bit mantissa?
questions.feedback: Six stored bits plus one temporary sign bit = seven.

blocks.title: Work through the method
blocks.text: Check the field widths before starting. Use the worked examples to guide each calculation, then read the feedback.

questions.feedback: Two right shifts compensate for increasing exponent 1 to 3.
The mantissa sum needs right rescaling; exponent rises to 4.
Copy the leading 1. This halves the signed mantissa for alignment.

questions.prompt: Add 011000 0011 and 010000 0010. Choose the normalised 6+4 result.
questions.feedback: 6 + 2 = 8. Align 010000 to 001000 at exponent 3; sum rescaling gives 0.5 × 16.

questions.prompt: Add 101100 0011 and 011000 0001. Choose the normalised 6+4 result.
questions.feedback: −5 + 1.5 = −3.5. Align, add to get −0.4375 at exponent 3, then normalise to −0.875 at exponent 2.

questions.prompt: Can 32.5 be stored exactly with a six-bit mantissa and four-bit exponent?
questions.feedback: At this scale the representable step is 2; 32.5 lies between representable values.
options: Yes: normalisation restores all lost bits

writing.prompt: Explain why exponent alignment uses an arithmetic right shift for a negative mantissa, and why guard bits may be needed.
writing.model: Alignment increases the smaller exponent and divides its mantissa by two for each step, preserving the operand’s value when no precision is lost. An arithmetic right shift repeats the leading 1 of a negative mantissa so its sign is preserved. Guard bits retain low-order working bits that would otherwise be discarded. The final stored width may still require rounding, so guard bits do not guarantee an exact result.
checklist: I linked exponent increase to compensating mantissa division.
I distinguished working guard bits from final precision.

questions.prompt: Mantissas can be added directly even if their exponents differ.
questions.feedback: Align exponents first so place values match.

questions.prompt: Right-rescaling an oversized mantissa sum requires increasing the exponent.
questions.feedback: This compensates for dividing the mantissa by two.

questions.prompt: Normalisation can restore non-zero bits already discarded during alignment.
questions.feedback: Lost information cannot be recovered by shifting.
